<reason>Elite debate on both sides. A was more vivid (Quechua vignette, "hierarchy with a bilingual face," "extinctions cannot be rerouted") and asked the sharper pressure questions, exposing the promissory nature of B's reforms. But B won the analytical war on the motion's actual decision rule — net harm. B landed multiple hits A never answered: (1) A's own epistemic-flattening argument undermines the machine-translation alternative A relies on; (2) translating finished documents is not equivalent to live collaboration via a shared working language, damaging A's "benefits are portable" premise; (3) "permanent describes severity, not probability," and A never established the extinction chain for small languages as opposed to contingent domestic-policy failures; (4) B caught A overclaiming the concession in the closing ("we conceded unequal burdens — not inevitable extinction, and certainly not net harm"). A's strongest answers (status gradient can't be outbid; Finnish is another state-protected language) were substantive but left B's symmetry argument standing: both fixes are speculative, and A's alternative needs the same institutions while inheriting the same flattening risks. A proved real, conceded harms; B showed A never established that those harms outweigh the access and coordination capacity, and damaged A's central weighing premise more than A damaged B's.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2: the double catch that PRO's translation alternative still requires the human judgment needed to prevent the very epistemic flattening PRO complains about, and that a translated document is not a research collaboration — two structural hits on PRO's "portable benefits" thesis that went unanswered through the closings.</best_rebuttal>
